newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl confident on NATO despite Moscow demands.
newsitem.headline: Kohl confident on NATO despite Moscow demands.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Thursday he had concrete ideas to convince Moscow to accept NATO's eastward expansion and was optimistic Russian leaders would accept the move after open and cooperative negotiations.
Kohl told journalists Moscow still clearly opposed NATO's plan to include former Warsaw Pact countries but it could not have a veto right over what its neighbours did.
He said a series of tough anti-NATO statements made in Moscow this week did not change his views at all.

The chancellor, who visited Boris Yeltsin last Saturday, also said the Russian president was alert and determined to resume work when he saw him. They plan to speak again by telephone on Friday or over the weekend.
Yeltsin was admitted to hospital on Wednesday suffering from the first signs of pneumonia.
"I am optimistic on the basis of very concrete considerations which I of course do not want to name now," Kohl said at his annual New Year's news conference.
"I am convinced that, if we work together, we will find a resonable balance (of interests) and there is a possibility to implement this NATO expansion into the east together," he said.
On Tuesday, Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel talked of a broad array of issues he thought Moscow would seek concessions on in exchange for accepting NATO expansion.
These included the CFE conventional arms reduction treaty, the START-2 nuclear arms treaty, Moscow's role in the Group of Seven industrialised states and economic aid for Russia.

Kohl said Germany, which plays an important role in NATO's approach to the Russians because of its good relations with Moscow, supported expansion and opposed letting any country have a veto over what its neighbours did.
"If we introduced that in Europe, that would have terrible results," he warned, adding that he was also against delaying the expansion because positions are now so far apart.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Wednesday repeated Moscow's opposition to NATO expansion and said it wanted the right to joint decision-making with western countries on what it considers its vital interests.
Asked about this, Kohl only said it was one of many reactions to the NATO plan heard in east and west. "It changes nothing of what I have just said," he added.
Western diplomats say Primakov's plan would give Moscow influence over alliance decisions and worry east European states seeking a NATO shield against against Russian power.

Primakov also insisted on an updating of the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, which sets limits on where and how many conventional arms signatories can have. NATO has already agreed in principle to do this.

"There is still great mistrust among the Russian people and politicians against this NATO expansion," Kohl said. "After the end of the Cold War and the fall of the Berlin Wall, we don't want to put up new border posts and psychological walls."
He repeatedly stressed that talks with Russia had to be talks between friends and partners. He also said NATO would have to talk with Ukraine about its expansion plans.
Kohl said Yeltsin had clearly been suffering from a cold during their meeting.
"He's convalescing. He's not in same physical state as last year, but it was clear he has good chance if he takes care of himself," the chancellor said.

Kohl added: "He was totally mentally alert. He discussed the issues with me without lots of notes for two hours. One thing is very important. He wants to carry out the duties of his office. There is no sign of resignation there at all."
